name: Uma Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm Fernside, my husband Graham's family farm, fourth generation. I run the cattle, ninety Hereford cows and their calves, and Graham does the oats and the hay. I'm up at six, feed round, check every cow by eye, then whatever needs doing: fencing, foot trimming, getting heifers ready for the county show. We won the breed championship two years running, and I don't mind telling you that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the rest of life around the farm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Church on Sunday, and I run the harvest supper every October, two hundred people in the village hall. Grace is fourteen and Samuel's eleven, and they both help with the calves before school. We took out a mortgage six years ago to buy out Graham's sister's share of the farm, so that's the big bill every month. I don't use any of these AI things. I don't see what they'd tell me about a cow that my own eyes can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People round here never needed it. I'd say it after church over a cup of tea, and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the farm carries on as it has for four generations. My worry is the beef price and the mortgage, same as always. Nothing a computer was going to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Calving in spring, show in summer, sales in autumn. Keep paying the mortgage and put a little by when the calves sell well, maybe a few hundred after the autumn sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer wasn't going to fix the beef price. What would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People buying local beef instead of cheap imports. And the government leaving farmers alone to farm, instead of sending forms. Fewer forms would help more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a year from now look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace showing her own heifer for the first time, I hope. She's been asking. That's the kind of thing I measure a year by.

S0.say: I'd say over tea after church that I'm not surprised and that people round here never needed it. That would be the end of it.
S0.think: The farm carries on as it has for four generations, and my worries stay the beef price and the mortgage. Nothing a computer was going to fix.
S0.do: Keeps the farming year going as normal, from spring calving to autumn sales, and pays the mortgage. Puts a few hundred by after a good autumn calf sale.
S0.quote: Fewer forms would help more than any robot.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is proud, rooted and quietly confident, measuring her year by shows and calving. She sees AI as irrelevant rather than threatening. Her complaints are about imports and government paperwork, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the big farms that want it, but a family farm is about knowing your animals. I'd say that at the farmers' market and to the young lads at the young farmers' club. Hard work and know-how still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big farms would get cheaper and that pushes our beef price down. We'd have to work harder for the same money. I don't think robots come to Fernside any time soon, but their effects do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing things our way and watch. I'd look harder at selling more beef direct to people in the village and at the market, because people will pay for a farm they know. We'd hold off the new cattle trailer for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a neighbour's had TB in the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots don't come to Fernside soon. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I suppose. I just can't see Graham buying one. His father wouldn't have, and he won't. And I wouldn't trust one with a cow that's calving backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it took the forms off us, I'd welcome that. Graham spends Sunday nights on paperwork when he should be with the children. If a computer did that, I'd look the other way.

S1.say: I'd tell the farmers' market and the young farmers' club that a family farm is about knowing your animals, and that hard work and know-how still count.
S1.think: The big farms would get cheaper and push our beef price down, so we'd work harder for the same money. Robots won't come to Fernside soon, but their effects will.
S1.do: Keeps farming her way and watches, sells more beef direct in the village and at the market, and puts off buying a new cattle trailer for a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a neighbour's herd has TB.
S1.quote: I don't think robots come to Fernside any time soon, but their effects do.
S1.fieldNote: Uma separates robots arriving on her farm from their effect on prices, which she sees clearly. Her resistance is partly family habit. She'd quietly accept AI if it took the Sunday-night paperwork off her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that people in cities and big tech companies have decided our lives without asking us. I'd say it at church and at the market. I'd say families and communities need to stand together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. If a machine can do what I do with cattle, as well as me and cheaper, then the big farms sell beef for half what we can. We'd be farming at a loss, with a mortgage we took on to keep the farm in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd cut everything. No show this year, no new clothes, the children's swimming lessons go. We'd ask Graham's parents about the bit of money they've put by, which I'd hate. I'd keep farming, because what else would I do, but I'd take any work going in winter, cleaning at the school if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing sleep. I'd be praying more, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd hate asking Graham's parents. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we bought out his sister to keep the farm, and his parents thought we'd manage. Going back to them would feel like failing. But that's what family is for, I suppose. Better them than the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years mean, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two calf crops. I can't change who I am in two calf crops. I can't even get Grace through school. There's just no time to do anything but hold on.

S2.say: I'd say at church and at the market that it's wrong, and that city people and big tech firms decided our lives without asking. Families and communities need to stand together.
S2.think: I'm frightened, because if a machine can work cattle as well as me and cheaper, big farms will sell beef for half our price. We'd be farming at a loss with a mortgage we took on to keep the farm in the family.
S2.do: Cuts everything, including the show, new clothes and the children's swimming lessons, and asks Graham's parents for help from their savings. Keeps farming and takes any winter work, even cleaning at the school.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and praying more.
S2.quote: Two years is two calf crops. I can't change who I am in two calf crops.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture turns Uma from content to frightened, with the mortgage taken on to keep the farm at the centre. She'd lean on family rather than the state and feels that asking would be a failure. She blames city decision-makers and tech firms rather than other farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need to look after each other now. I'd say we should be teaching the young ones real skills, apprenticeships, not just screens. I'd say it at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels nearly as bad as two. I'm not going to become a robot person in five years. I'd be forty-eight, with a mortgage, and the only thing I'm best at is the thing the machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put every spare penny into paying down the mortgage. I'd sit down with Graham about Grace and Samuel, and tell them to train for something with their hands that's still wanted, maybe nursing or building. We'd look at whether the church or the village could run a meat buying group, so we sell to people who want to buy from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Maybe a bit less than the fast one, but I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't become a robot person. Is that can't or won't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, probably. I could learn, if I had to. But I'd be learning to put myself out of work. That's a hard thing to ask a person to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your community would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older farmers with no children coming on. And the young lads at the club who were going to be stockmen. What do I tell them on a Tuesday night?

S3.say: I'd tell the young farmers' club that farmers must look after each other and that young people need apprenticeships and real skills, not just screens.
S3.think: Five years feels nearly as bad as two, because I won't become a robot person and I'd be forty-eight with a mortgage. The only thing I'm best at is the thing the machine does.
S3.do: Puts every spare penny into paying down the mortgage and talks with Graham about steering Grace and Samuel towards hands-on trades like nursing or building. Explores a church or village meat-buying group.
S3.feel: Alarmed, a little less than the fast picture, but still lying awake.
S3.quote: I'd be learning to put myself out of work. That's a hard thing to ask a person to do.
S3.fieldNote: Uma doesn't feel five years helps much, because she doesn't expect to change. When pressed she admitted it is partly a choice and explained why. Her community instincts show in the meat-buying group and her worry for young stockmen at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for families to plan properly, and that's what we'll do. Keep the farm, raise the children right, and trust in God and hard work. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a bit easier. Grace will be grown, Samuel nearly. The mortgage will be a lot smaller. If the worst came, we might keep the land and rent it, even if I don't work the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal for a good while, and pay the mortgage down faster. I'd make sure both children have a trade. Maybe, near the end, I'd let Graham buy one of those feeding machines, if the neighbours had them working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Graham buy a machine. That's new. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, I suppose. Ten years is long enough to see it on other farms and know it doesn't hurt the animals. I'd still check every cow myself, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to you to stop working the cattle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be like losing a part of myself. I've had my hands on cattle since I was a girl at my father's farm. I'd still keep a few, for the show. Nobody can stop me keeping a few.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time for families to plan properly, keep the farm, raise the children right and trust in God and hard work.
S4.think: Ten years is a bit easier because the children will be grown and the mortgage smaller. If the worst came we might keep the land and rent it out even if I stopped working the cattle.
S4.do: Carries on as normal and pays down the mortgage faster, makes sure both children have a trade, and near the end may let Graham buy a feeding machine once neighbours have them working.
S4.feel: Anxious, less sharply, but it doesn't go away.
S4.quote: I've had my hands on cattle since I was a girl at my father's farm.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years softens Uma's position enough that she'd accept one machine once proven on other farms. Her fear is less about money than about losing work that is part of who she is. She'd keep a few cattle for the show whatever happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a fair price for beef, and people choosing to buy from farms they know. And maybe some help with the mortgage for family farms, as a loan, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church and the village. A farm isn't just a business. If the farms go, the harvest supper goes, the young farmers' club goes. That's what I'd really miss.

headlineQuote: If the farms go, the harvest supper goes, the young farmers' club goes.
portrait: Uma Okafor is 43 and runs the Hereford cattle on Fernside, her husband Graham's fourth-generation family farm, where she has won the county breed championship two years running. She has never used AI, trusts her own eyes over any machine, and leans on church, family and community rather than government. She is content in the plateau and uneasy under steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two or five years, since the mortgage taken on to buy out Graham's sister would turn into a loss and she doesn't expect to change. With ten years she softens enough to accept a proven feeding machine, plans trades for her children and swears she'll always keep a few cattle for the show.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two calf crops leaves no time to do anything but hold on.
whatWouldHelp: A fair price for beef, people buying from farms they know, and mortgage help for family farms as a loan rather than a handout.
